prize_parts.citation: for their analysis of how constitutions, electoral rules and state capacity shape fiscal policy and economic development

statement.case_for: Persson, Tabellini and Besley turned the study of political institutions into a core part of economics. They gave a formal account of how electoral systems, forms of government and state capacity determine fiscal policy, redistribution and public-goods provision, and they confronted that account with cross-country and historical evidence. The work is a coherent programme whose theory and evidence have been taken up in macroeconomics, public economics and development. It is also mature: three decades of replication, extension and use in graduate training. Persson and Tabellini form the core pair through their joint research programme and book, and Besley's work on state capacity and political accountability is closely complementary. The three-name limit therefore fits this candidate better than it fits most others on the shortlist, where credit is spread across more people.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with the 2024 prize for work on institutions and prosperity. Some members may feel the territory has recently been covered. A second concern is identification. Parts of the cross-country evidence on constitutional effects rest on weaker causal designs than the evidence behind the leading alternatives. The candidate also has the thinnest opening support on the shortlist among the front-runners. That is not evidence about merit, but it shows I have not yet persuaded colleagues who rank other topics higher. Attribution is clean among the credited names, but others outside the list also made contributions to political economics, and a three-name prize cannot reflect all of them.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B021 third and credits it with creating modern political economics. He flags that causal identification is weaker in parts of the cross-country evidence and that the 2024 institutions prize may overlap.
responses.response: I accept the identification point and have listed it as my own uncertainty. It applies most to the early cross-country regressions on constitutions and electoral rules. The theory and the later evidence on state capacity are less exposed to it. On overlap, I see the 2024 prize and B021 as complementary rather than duplicative. The 2024 work asked whether inclusive institutions cause long-run prosperity, using colonial history for identification. It also explained institutional persistence through commitment problems. B021 asks a different question: how specific constitutional and electoral rules map into policy choices inside a political system. I grant that the committee could still treat them as one theme, and I regard that as the main risk to this candidacy.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B015 first as the strongest case on the list and B021 second. He notes that the Prize has recently recognised related institutions research and that the committee may see the programme as several contributions rather than one.
responses.response: I agree that B015 is exceptionally influential and mature, and I keep it as an alternative. My reservation is attribution, which Krusell also acknowledges. Eight credited names compete for three places, and Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets have strong claims. B021 does not have that problem to the same degree. On whether it is one discovery or several, I think the common thread is a single question: how rules and institutional design determine policy outcomes. The Persson-Tabellini programme and Besley's work on state capacity answer it with shared formal tools. I cannot rule out that a committee will read it as separate strands, and that leaves a real uncertainty.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B050 first and restricts it to Kiyotaki and Moore. He argues this is the cleanest attribution, because the financial-accelerator line is partly covered by the 2022 prize. He also concedes that direct empirical identification of the amplification mechanism is mixed.
responses.response: I agree with the two-name restriction and made the same choice in my own B050 proposal. It is also why I keep B050 as an alternative rather than a lower-ranked afterthought. We differ on ordering. The identification caveat Strömberg raises for B050, a mechanism that is theoretically foundational but less cleanly identified, is close to the caveat I accept for B021. I do not think it separates the two candidates. The question that does is whether the committee values a collateral-constraint mechanism for credit cycles over a unified account of political institutions and fiscal policy. That is a judgement about the field and not something the evidence settles.

responses.point: Boppart ranks the heterogeneous-firm trade model first. He argues it changed trade theory, fits firm-level microdata, and has two decades of confirmation, though the gains-from-trade magnitudes are sensitive to assumptions.
responses.response: I agree that B038 is empirically disciplined and mature, and its link to microdata is stronger than anything B021 can offer on identification. I do not rank it above B021 because of what each shows. The firm-heterogeneity work reshaped one subfield's workhorse model. B021 reached across several fields: macroeconomics, public economics and comparative politics. Boppart himself notes that Helpman's credit is split with another ballot item and that the 2008 prize covered earlier trade theory. I take those points seriously, but they bear on prize design more than on the quality of the work. I do not think B038 is weaker, and I would not object strongly to it. I just rank it below B021.

uncertainties: How far the 2024 institutions prize reduces the committee's appetite for a prize on political economics.
Whether cross-country evidence on constitutional and electoral effects is credible enough for the causal claims in the citation.
Whether the programme is read as one discovery or as several strands.
How to weigh Besley's contribution against that of other contributors outside the credited list.
How much weight should go to B015, whose maturity and policy influence are very large but whose attribution among eight names is unresolved.
statement.conflict_note: My field, political science, is close to the subject matter of B021: comparative democratisation, quality of government and state-building. I also gave the 2024 presentation speech on institutions and prosperity, so I am familiar with the neighbouring prize and may overstate either its distinctness from B021 or its overlap with it. My profile lists no co-authorship with Besley, Tabellini or Torsten Persson. It names a co-author 'Persson' on corruption work but gives no first name, and I do not identify that person with Torsten Persson. Colleagues' openings state that Torsten Persson is at the IIES at Stockholm University, where I also hold a chair in a different department. The profile does not confirm his affiliation. I disclose these connections for the committee to weigh and do not adjudicate them.
